extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (mathematical induction, recursion, and related number theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples on using ordinary and strong induction, recursion, the well-ordering principle, and related proof strategies (existence proofs, disjunctions, recursive sequences, transitive closures). Includes scratch-work heuristics and typical proof structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form ∀n ∈ N P(n): prove a base case (usually P(0)) and prove the induction step P(n) → P(n+1) by assuming an arbitrary n and the inductive hypothesis P(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case gets the process started; the induction step shows the process can be continued from one number to the next. In formal terms: show P(0) holds, then show for arbitrary n that P(n) implies P(n+1); then conclude ∀n P(n). Work out the details if any step is not immediately clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen the goal to make induction work
rubrics_metrics.description: If a direct induction on the desired statement is awkward or fails, replace the original goal by a seemingly stronger statement that is easier to carry through the induction (e.g., prove (1+x)^n ≥ 1 + nx instead of (1+x)^n > nx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the strengthened statement looks harder, the induction step may work smoothly on it (as in multiplying the inductive hypothesis by a positive factor). After proving the stronger statement, deduce the original claim as a corollary if appropriate (here, 1+nx > nx). Be open to proving a different but stronger invariant that is preserved by the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction for existential statements — construct explicit witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the goal has existential quantifiers (∃q∃r ...), plan to produce explicit witnesses, using simple choices for trivial cases and using the inductive hypothesis to build witnesses for larger n (e.g., in the division algorithm choose q=0,r=n when n<m; otherwise use the inductive hypothesis applied to n−m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think constructively: find formulas or constructions for the witnesses. Use the inductive hypothesis on an appropriate smaller input (which may not be n−1) to obtain partial witnesses and then modify them to get witnesses for n. Work out and justify cases (e.g., n<m versus n≥m).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction (complete induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove ∀n[(∀k < n P(k)) → P(n)]. In practice: let n be arbitrary, assume P(k) for every k < n, and prove P(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No separate base case is strictly required because plugging n=0 yields a vacuous assumption and thus P(0) follows; nevertheless, initial cases are often checked explicitly for clarity. Use strong induction when the proof of P(n) needs information about several smaller values, not just n−1.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction when the induction step requires hypotheses about multiple earlier values (e.g., recurrences depending on two prior terms, or proofs that use division as repeated subtraction so you need n−m rather than n−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: division algorithm (uses n−m), Fibonacci formulas (depend on Fn−1 and Fn−2). If the recursive/structural definition references earlier-than-previous elements, choose strong induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing the right smaller index to apply the inductive hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In an inductive proof, the appropriate smaller instance to plug into the inductive hypothesis may be other values than n−1 (for example, use n−m in the division algorithm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the structure of the problem (e.g., think of division as repeated subtraction) to identify which smaller k < n to use. Try candidate k’s in scratch work to see which yields a usable inductive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving disjunctions during induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the goal is a disjunction (A ∨ B), a standard strategy is to assume the negation of one disjunct (¬A) and prove the other (B); in inductive proofs this often pairs with existential introductions derived from the assumption (e.g., to show n is prime or a product of primes, assume n is not prime and obtain factors a and b to which the inductive hypothesis applies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply existential instantiation on 'n is not prime' to obtain factors, then apply the inductive hypothesis to those factors to conclude the required disjunction. Structuring a proof of a disjunction this way often simplifies the induction step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle (use and equivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element. This principle can be proved by strong induction and used as an alternative to induction in many proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the well-ordering principle to choose a minimal counterexample or minimal element of a nonempty set and derive a contradiction (common tactic in proofs by minimal counterexample). Alternatively, prove the well-ordering principle by strong induction when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction using minimal counterexample (well-ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a negative statement, assume the contrary and consider the set of counterexamples; by well-ordering choose the minimal counterexample and show a smaller counterexample exists, yielding contradiction (as in the proof that √2 is irrational by choosing minimal denominator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This often yields a short, elegant contradiction: manipulate the minimal counterexample to produce a strictly smaller one, contradicting minimality. Explain why the set of counterexamples is nonempty under the contrary assumption and why you can pick a minimal element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match induction to the recursion depth of definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving facts about recursively defined objects (sequences, relations), choose an induction scheme that mirrors the recursion: e.g., Fibonacci numbers depend on two earlier terms, so use strong induction or check two base cases separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle base cases corresponding to the independent initial values of the recursion (e.g., F0 and F1). In the induction step, assume the formula for all required prior indices and use the recursive relation to derive the formula for n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scratch-work / proof planning for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing the formal proof, do scratch work: restate the goal in logical form, decide which form of induction to use, identify the inductive hypothesis, and experiment with small values to discover patterns or appropriate choices for witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch likely choices (e.g., for witnesses q and r), decide case splits (n<m vs n≥m), and determine which k to substitute into the inductive hypothesis. Use this planning to make the formal proof straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive closure via iterative composition (Rn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define R1 = R and Rn+1 = Rn ◦ R. The transitive closure of R is S = ⋃_{n∈Z+} Rn. Prove properties by induction: Lemma Rm+n = Rm ◦ Rn, S is transitive, and S is the smallest transitive relation containing R (i.e., any transitive T with R ⊆ T has S ⊆ T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove Rm+n = Rm ◦ Rn by induction on n using associativity of composition. To show minimality, prove by induction on n that Rn ⊆ T for any transitive T containing R. Name ⋃Rn as S and check the three requirements for transitive closure (contains R, transitive, minimal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use associativity when composing relations in inductive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When composing multiple relations (R ◦ R ◦ ... ◦ R), rely on associativity of composition to avoid parenthesis clutter and to justify equalities like (Rm ◦ Rn) ◦ R = Rm ◦ (Rn ◦ R) in inductive steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cite associativity when rearranging compositions in inductive arguments. This simplifies algebraic manipulations in proofs involving Rn and their compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat initial/base cases explicitly when recursion requires them
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if strong induction formally makes a separate base case unnecessary, many proofs still treat initial cases (n=0, n=1, ...) separately because recursive definitions often define a few initial values independently (e.g., Fibonacci requires checking n=0 and n=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify initial cases explicitly to ensure the inductive machinery can be started; explain their role as analogous to base cases in ordinary induction.
